claim: Social chemosignaling is a part of human behavior.
source: Social chemosignaling is a part of human behavior, but how chemosignals transfer from one individual to another is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on established scientific consensus.

claim: How chemosignals transfer from one individual to another is unknown.
source: Social chemosignaling is a part of human behavior, but how chemosignals transfer from one individual to another is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: The functional antecedents of handshaking behavior remain unclear.
source: In turn, humans greet each other with handshakes, but the functional antecedents of this behavior remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: 271 subjects were covertly filmed within a structured greeting event either with or without a handshake.
source: To ask whether handshakes are used to sample conspecific social chemosignals, we covertly filmed 271 subjects within a structured greeting event either with or without a handshake.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methodology used in the study.

claim: Humans often sniff their own hands.
source: We found that humans often sniff their own hands, and selectively increase this behavior after handshake.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the observational data collected in the study.

claim: Humans selectively increase hand-sniffing behavior after handshake.
source: We found that humans often sniff their own hands, and selectively increase this behavior after handshake.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the observational data collected in the study.

claim: After handshakes within gender, subjects increased sniffing of their own right shaking hand by more than 100%.
source: After handshakes within gender, subjects increased sniffing of their own right shaking hand by more than 100%.
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the experimental data.

claim: After handshakes across gender, subjects increased sniffing of their own left non-shaking hand by more than 100%.
source: In contrast, after handshakes across gender, subjects increased sniffing of their own left non-shaking hand by more than 100%.
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the experimental data.

claim: Tainting participants with unnoticed odors significantly altered the hand-sniffing effects.
source: Tainting participants with unnoticed odors significantly altered the effects, thus verifying their olfactory nature.
evidence: This describes the results of the odor-tainting control experiment.

claim: The odor-tainting experiment verified the olfactory nature of the hand-sniffing behavior.
source: Tainting participants with unnoticed odors significantly altered the effects, thus verifying their olfactory nature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from the tainting experiment.

claim: Handshaking may functionally serve active yet subliminal social chemosignaling.
source: Thus, handshaking may functionally serve active yet subliminal social chemosignaling, which likely plays a large role in ongoing human behavior.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Social chemosignaling likely plays a large role in ongoing human behavior.
source: Thus, handshaking may functionally serve active yet subliminal social chemosignaling, which likely plays a large role in ongoing human behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings and broader context.

claim: Social chemosignaling plays a large role in mammalian and particularly rodent behavior.
source: Social chemosignaling plays a large role in mammalian and particularly rodent behavior (Dulac and Torello, 2003; Keverne, 2005; Stowers and Marton, 2005; Brennan and Zufall, 2006; Kaur et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mammals typically greet each other with careful olfactory investigation.
source: and therefore mammals typically greet each other with careful olfactory investigation (Doty, 1986; Drea et al., 2002; Wesson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is mounting evidence for the role of social chemosignaling in ongoing human behavior.
source: Similarly, there is mounting evidence for the role of social chemosignaling in ongoing human behavior (McClintock, 2000; Wysocki and Preti, 2004; de Groot et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals drive menstrual synchrony.
source: Human social chemosignals drive menstrual synchrony (Stern and McClintock, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals serve in mate selection.
source: serve in mate selection (Jacob et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals convey fear.
source: convey fear (Chen et al., 2006; Zhou and Chen, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals drive pronounced hormonal modifications.
source: drive pronounced hormonal (Preti et al., 2003; Wyart et al., 2007; Gelstein et al., 2011) and behavioral (Jacob et al., 2001a; Bensafi et al., 2003) modifications
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals drive pronounced behavioral modifications.
source: drive pronounced hormonal (Preti et al., 2003; Wyart et al., 2007; Gelstein et al., 2011) and behavioral (Jacob et al., 2001a; Bensafi et al., 2003) modifications
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human social chemosignals alter brain activity.
source: and alter brain activity (Sobel et al., 1999; Jacob et al., 2001b; Savic et al., 2001, 2005; Lundström et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There remains controversy on the statistics of menstrual synchrony.
source: Although there remains controversy on the statistics of menstrual synchrony (Schank, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There is controversy on application of the term pheromone to instances of social chemosignaling in humans.
source: and on application of the term pheromone to instances of social chemosignaling in humans (Meredith, 2001; Wysocki and Preti, 2004; Doty, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: That humans emit odors that can influence behavior and perception in other humans is largely agreed upon.
source: that humans emit odors that can influence behavior and perception in other humans is largely agreed upon.
evidence: This reflects scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Unlike other mammals, humans do not engage in overt olfactory sampling and investigation of conspecifics.
source: Unlike other mammals, however, humans do not engage in overt olfactory sampling and investigation of conspecifics.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about human behavior compared to other mammals.

claim: Some human cultures include explicit olfactory sampling in stereotypical greeting behaviors.
source: Although some human cultures include explicit olfactory sampling in stereotypical greeting behaviors (Classen, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Common behaviors such as hugging and kissing provide ample opportunity for covert olfactory sampling.
source: and common behaviors such as hugging and kissing provide ample opportunity for covert olfactory sampling (Nicholson, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Human overt olfactory sampling and investigation of unfamiliar individuals is largely a taboo.
source: human overt olfactory sampling and investigation of unfamiliar individuals is largely a taboo.
evidence: This is stated as a cultural observation about human behavior.

claim: Handshaking is common across cultures and history.
source: Handshaking is common across cultures and history (Firth, 1972; Schiffrin, 1974)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The commonly cited notion of gesturing no weapons in the shaking hand has only limited scholarly support.
source: and the commonly cited notion of gesturing no weapons in the shaking hand has only limited scholarly support.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the scholarly literature.

claim: Handshakes are sufficient for the transfer of various pathogens.
source: Handshakes are sufficient for the transfer of various pathogens (Mela and Whitworth, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Handshakes are likely sufficient for the transfer of chemosignals.
source: and it is therefore likely that they are sufficient for the transfer of chemosignals as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathogen transfer finding.

claim: Gas-chromatography mass-spectrometry was used to sample surgical nitrile gloves before and after a handshake with the bare hand of 10 individuals.
source: To test whether the general type of molecules implicated in chemosignaling can also be transferred by handshake, we used gas-chromatography mass-spectrometry to sample surgical nitrile gloves before and after a handshake with the bare hand of 10 individuals (5F, mean age = 34.1 ± 5.6 years) (Figure 1A)
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Several peaks in the chromatograms were effectively transferred through handshake alone.
source: Examination of the resulting chromatograms (Figure 1B) revealed several peaks that were all effectively transferred through handshake alone.
evidence: This is a finding from the GCMS analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Squalene is a putative social chemosignaling component in several species including dogs.
source: such as squalene, which is a putative social chemosignaling component in several species including dogs (Apps et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Squalene is a putative social chemosignaling component in rats.
source: such as squalene, which is a putative social chemosignaling component in several species including dogs (Apps et al., 2012) and rats (Achiraman et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hexadecanoic acid is a putative social chemosignaling component in mammals.
source: hexadecanoic acid, which is a putative social chemosignaling component in both mammals (Briand et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hexadecanoic acid is a putative social chemosignaling component in insects.
source: hexadecanoic acid, which is a putative social chemosignaling component in both mammals (Briand et al., 2004) and insects (Tang et al., 1989)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Geranyl acetone is present in human secretions.
source: and geranyl acetone, which is present in human secretions (Gallagher et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Geranyl acetone was considered a social chemosignaling component in insects alone.
source: but to date was considered a social chemosignaling component in insects alone (Zarbin et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each of the three compounds (squalene, hexadecanoic acid, geranyl acetone) was transferred by handshake in all 10 of 10 subjects but not once in the control.
source: Each of these three compounds was transferred by handshake in all 10 of 10 subjects but not once in the control (all t[9] > 3.9, all p < 0.003).
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the GCMS experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: The three compounds detected were likely endogenous skin-bound molecules.
source: We therefore submitted this hand-soap to GCMS analysis as well, and did not detect any traces of the three above components. Thus, we conclude that these were likely endogenous skin-bound molecules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the control analysis of hand-soap.

claim: The act of handshaking is sufficient to transfer molecules of the type that are likely relevant to mammalian social chemosignaling.
source: These results do not imply that these molecules are necessarily social chemosignaling components in humans, but they do demonstrate that the act of handshaking is sufficient to transfer molecules of the type that are likely relevant to mammalian social chemosignaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GCMS experimental data.

claim: 175 subjects were recruited into the greeting paradigm.
source: We therefore recruited 175 subjects into this paradigm (84F, mean age = 26.49 ± 3.69 years), who each shook hands with one of 20 different experimenters (13F, mean age = 35.24 ± 6.38 years).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: The correlation between raters regarding duration of face-touches was r = 0.96, p < 0.0001.
source: The correlation between raters regarding duration of face-touches was r = 0.96, p < 0.0001 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a statistical result demonstrating inter-rater reliability, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 22 subjects were omitted from further analysis due to non-compliance.
source: Through this process, we also omitted 22 subjects from further analysis due to non-compliance (typically using a cell-phone during the experiment), retaining 153 subjects, 80 who experienced greets with handshake, and 73 who experienced greets without handshake.
evidence: This describes the data cleaning process.

claim: Of 153 subjects, 85 (55.55%) touched their nose with their hand at least once during baseline before the greet.
source: Of 153 subjects, 85 (55.55%) touched their nose with their hand at least once during baseline before the greet.
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the observational data.

claim: The average time of a hand at the nose across ∼80 s was 5.38 ± 15.7 s for the right hand, and 12.33 ± 23.81 s for the left hand.
source: The average time of a hand at the nose across these ∼80 s was 5.38 ± 15.7 s for the right hand, and 12.33 ± 23.81 s for the left hand.
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the observational data.

claim: The left over right hand preference for nose touching was significant (F[1,151] = 8.14, p = 0.005).
source: An analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed that this left over right hand preference was significant (F[1,151] = 8.14, p = 0.005)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: There was no difference across genders in hand-to-nose touching behavior (F[1,151] = 0.3, p = 0.86).
source: and there was no difference across genders in this behavior (F[1,151] = 0.3, p = 0.86) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Idle subjects had a hand at the vicinity of their nose for 22.14% of the time.
source: Combined, this amounts to ∼17 s, in other words idle subjects had a hand (either right or left) at the vicinity of their nose for 22.14% of the time.
evidence: This is a calculated finding from the observational data.

claim: Facial touching was mostly in regions at or under the nose.
source: This representation revealed that facial touching was mostly in regions at or under the nose, rendering the touching hand potentially well placed for olfactory exploration (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Facial self-touching has been considered a form of displacement stress response.
source: Whereas facial self-touching has been considered a form of displacement stress response (Troisi, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: 33 additional subjects were tested with concurrent measurement of nasal airflow.
source: Although we think that the video data are strongly supportive of this view (see online Video 1), to further estimate whether bringing the hand to the nose is associated with olfactory exploration, we repeated the task in 33 additional subjects (26F, mean age = 23.84 ± 5.36 years) with concurrent measurement of nasal airflow.
evidence: This describes an additional control experiment.

claim: When a hand was at the vicinity of the nose, nasal airflow more than doubled over baseline.
source: We found that when a hand was at the vicinity of the nose, nasal airflow more than doubled over baseline (baseline flow = 112.75 ± 75.56 ml/s, hand-at-face flow = 237.81 ± 220.82 ml/s, t[16] = 2.37, p = 0.03) (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the nasal airflow experiment shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When subjects brought their hand to their nose, they concurrently sniffed.
source: In other words, when subjects brought their hand to their nose, they concurrently sniffed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nasal airflow data.

claim: Both men and women significantly increased exploration of the hand that shook after shaking hands within gender.
source: In brief, this analysis primarily revealed that both men and women significantly increased exploration of the hand that shook after shaking hands within gender.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of the observational data.

claim: After shaking hands across gender, both men and women decreased right (shaking) hand exploration to a level below baseline.
source: By contrast, after shaking hands across gender, both men and women decreased right (shaking) hand exploration to a level below baseline, yet increased exploration of the left (non-shaking) hand to significantly above baseline.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of the observational data.

claim: After shaking hands across gender, both men and women increased exploration of the left (non-shaking) hand to significantly above baseline.
source: By contrast, after shaking hands across gender, both men and women decreased right (shaking) hand exploration to a level below baseline, yet increased exploration of the left (non-shaking) hand to significantly above baseline.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis of the observational data.

claim: The ANOVA revealed a main effect of experimenter gender (F[1,77] = 7.28, p = 0.009).
source: The ANOVA revealed a main effect of experimenter gender (F[1,77] = 7.28, p = 0.009)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: The ANOVA revealed an overwhelming three-way interaction (F[1,77] = 37.79, p < 0.0001).
source: and an overwhelming three-way interaction (F[1,77] = 37.79, p < 0.0001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: Handshakes from male experimenters elicited increased ensuing sampling of the left non-shaking hand in both men and women equally.
source: The main effect reflected that in both men and women equally (F[1,77] = 0.19, p = 0.66), handshakes from male experimenters elicited increased ensuing sampling of the left non-shaking hand (mean Fexp = −0.82 ± 17.55 s, mean Mexp = 7.54 ± 14.95, t[79] = 2.29, p = 0.025, non-parametric reanalysis: Mann–Whitney U, Z = 3.17, p = 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis with non-parametric confirmation.

claim: Exploration of the right shaking hand increased after shaking the hand of an individual from the same gender.
source: The three-way interaction reflected that for both men and women equally (F[1,77] = 0.18, p = 0.67), exploration of the right shaking hand increased after shaking the hand of an individual from the same gender, yet decreased after shaking the hand of an individual from the opposite gender (within gender = 7.34 ± 8.16 s, across gender = −5.79 ± 18.99 s, t[79] = 4.02, p = 0.0001, non-parametric reanalysis: Mann–Whitney U, Z = 6.05, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Individuals significantly increased right hand exploration following same gender greets that contained a handshake by 135.99%.
source: These subjects (within gender with handshake) shifted in right shaking hand sampling from an expected −5.39 ± 15.29 s (expected = change following no-handshake greet) to 2.14 ± 8.1 s (change following handshake greet), that is, a 135.99% increase.
evidence: This is a calculated finding from the experimental data.

claim: Sampling of the left non-shaking hand decreased after shaking the hand of an individual from the same gender, yet increased after shaking the hand of an individual from the opposite gender.
source: In contrast, sampling of the left non-shaking hand decreased after shaking the hand of an individual from the same gender, yet increased after shaking the hand of an individual from the opposite gender (within gender = −4.86 ± 17.5 s, across gender = 10.87 ± 11.89 s, t[79] = 4.74, p < 0.0001, non-parametric reanalysis: Mann–Whitney U, Z = 5.62, p < 0.0001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Subjects in the across gender with handshake condition shifted in left non-shaking hand sampling by 139.24% increase.
source: These subjects (across gender with handshake) shifted in left non-shaking hand sampling from an expected −7.95 ± 28.33 s (expected = change following no-handshake greet) to 2.91 ± 11.84 s (change following handshake greet), that is, a 139.24% increase.
evidence: This is a calculated finding from the experimental data.

claim: The right hand increase in touching following within gender handshakes was directly at the vicinity of the nose.
source: We found that the right hand increase in touching following within gender handshakes was directly at the vicinity of the nose (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average latency following greet onset in those subjects that explored the shaking hand was 25.65 ± 16.48 s.
source: The average latency following greet onset in those subjects that explored the shaking hand was 25.65 ± 16.48 s (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantified finding from the latency analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Women experimenters trended towards eliciting faster sampling responses regardless of subject gender.
source: An ANOVA on latency change scores revealed a trend towards a main effect of experimenter gender (F[1,57] = 3.57, p = 0.06) reflecting that women experimenters trended towards eliciting faster sampling responses regardless of subject gender (change from condition-specific baseline, women experimenters = −14.27 ± 29.72 s, men experimenters = 0.36 ± 29.43 s, t[59] = 1.92, p < 0.06).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the latency analysis.

claim: Although two experimenters drove more ensuing exploration than others, these differences did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Moreover, individual comparisons revealed that although two experimenters drove more ensuing exploration than others (both p < 0.05), these differences did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the individual experimenter analysis.

claim: 15 of the 153 subjects and two of the 20 experimenters were left-handed.
source: Consistent with population distribution, 15 of the 153 subjects and two of the 20 experimenters were left-handed.
evidence: This describes the handedness distribution in the sample.

claim: Three of four left-handed subjects (75%) in the 'with handshake within gender' condition increased investigation of the shaking hand after handshake.
source: This retained four left-handed subjects in the 'with handshake within gender' condition, three of which (75%) increased investigation of the shaking hand (right) after handshake.
evidence: This is a finding from the handedness subgroup analysis.

claim: The effect in left-handed subjects is not statistically different from right-handed subjects (X2 = 2.12, p = 0.14).
source: This reflects a trend towards a stronger effect in left-handed subjects, but this difference is not statistically different from the remaining right-handed subjects (X2 = 2.12, p = 0.14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the handedness analysis.

claim: Subjects were often alone in the room when they engaged in the measured hand-sniffing behavior.
source: As noted above, mean greet duration was 20 ± 8 s, and mean sample latency was 25.65 ± 16.48 s. In other words, subjects were often alone in the room when they engaged in the measured behavior, and therefore this was mostly not a direct concurrent response to the presence of the experimenter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing data.

claim: Three experimental groups were added: one where women experimenters were tainted with AND (n = 22), one with EST (n = 20), and one with commercial unisex perfume (n = 21).
source: We added three experimental groups: one where women experimenters were tainted with the putative male social chemosignal 4,16-androstadien-3-one (AND) (Savic et al., 2001; Huoviala and Rantala, 2013) (n = 22), one where women experimenters were tainted with the putative female social chemosignal estra-1,3,5(10),16-tetraen-3-ol (EST) (Savic et al., 2001; Huoviala and Rantala, 2013) (n = 20), and one where women experimenters were tainted with a commercial unisex perfume (CK-be) (n = 21).
evidence: This describes the design of the odor-tainting control experiment.

claim: 4,16-androstadien-3-one (AND) is a putative male social chemosignal.
source: one where women experimenters were tainted with the putative male social chemosignal 4,16-androstadien-3-one (AND) (Savic et al., 2001; Huoviala and Rantala, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Estra-1,3,5(10),16-tetraen-3-ol (EST) is a putative female social chemosignal.
source: one where women experimenters were tainted with the putative female social chemosignal estra-1,3,5(10),16-tetraen-3-ol (EST) (Savic et al., 2001; Huoviala and Rantala, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: An ANOVA with factors of hand and condition revealed a significant interaction of hand and condition (F[3,81] = 4.35, p < 0.007).
source: An ANOVA with factors of hand (L/R) and condition (AND/EST/CKB/clean) revealed no main effects, but a significant interaction of hand and condition (F[3,81] = 4.35, p < 0.007) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the odor-tainting experiment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a decrease in self exploration of the shaking hand following tainting with the putative chemosignals compared to increased self exploration when no taint was used or after tainting with perfume.
source: Planned comparisons revealed that this reflected a decrease in self exploration of the shaking hand following tainting with the putative chemosignals compared to increased self exploration when no taint was used or after tainting with perfume (mean clean = 2.5 ± 10.1 s, mean EST = −7.2 ± 18.2, mean AND = −1.93 ± 9.5, mean perfume = 5.29 ± 13; clean vs EST: t[40] = 2.16, p = 0.04, perfume vs EST: t[39] = 2.53, p < 0.02, perfume vs AND: t[41] = 2.1, p = 0.04. Non-parametric reanalysis: Mann–Whitney U, clean vs EST Z = 1.97, p < 0.05, perfume vs EST Z = 2.2, p < 0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the planned comparisons in the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: There was an increase in self-exploration of the left non-shaking hand following tainting with putative chemosignals compared to a decrease when no taint was used and no change after tainting with perfume.
source: In contrast, a mirror image effect was evident in the non-shaking left hand. Here, there was an increase in self-exploration following tainting with putative chemosignals compared to a decrease when no taint was used and no change after tainting with perfume (mean clean = −5.7 ± 17.8 s, mean EST = 4 ± 8.8, mean AND = 2.47 ± 16.42, mean perfume = −0.12 ± 13.48; clean vs EST: t[40] = 2.2, p < 0.04. Non-parametric reanalysis: Mann–Whitney U, clean vs EST Z = 2.38, p < 0.02, clean vs AND Z = 2.36, p < 0.02)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the planned comparisons in the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: In the perfume condition, only 7 of 21 subjects noticed an odor.
source: In the perfume condition, only 7 of 21 subjects noticed an odor (binomial cumulative P[X ≥ 7] = 0.96)
evidence: This is a finding from the exit questionnaire data.

claim: There was no difference in sampling behavior between those who did and did not notice an odor in the perfume condition.
source: and there was no difference in sampling behavior between those who did and did not notice an odor (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, X2 = 2.38, p = 0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the perfume condition analysis.

claim: In the EST condition, only 4 of 20 subjects noticed an odor.
source: Similarly, in the EST condition, only 4 of 20 subjects noticed an odor (Binomial cumulative P[X ≥ 4] = 0.99)
evidence: This is a finding from the exit questionnaire data.

claim: There was no difference in sampling behavior between those who did and did not notice an odor in the EST condition.
source: and here too there was no difference in sampling behavior between those who did and did not notice an odor (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, X2 = 1.8, p = 0.81).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the EST condition analysis.

claim: Odors had a pronounced influence on the behavior of self-exploration after handshake.
source: Taken together, the first hypothesis materialized, and odors had a pronounced influence on the behavior of self-exploration after handshake.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the odor-tainting experiment results.

claim: The odor influence on self-exploration persisted despite lack of awareness for the odor manipulation.
source: This influence remained consistent with the previously observed mirror behaviors of the left and right hands, and persisted despite lack of awareness for the odor manipulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the odor-tainting experiment results combined with the awareness data.

claim: There was no difference between AND and EST in their effects on hand-sniffing behavior.
source: In contrast, the second hypothesis did not materialize, and there was no difference between AND and EST in this respect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the odor-tainting experiment results.

claim: Human subjects repeatedly investigated their own hands, and this was often accompanied by overt sniffing.
source: A striking aspect of these observations was the extent of apparent olfactory self-exploration: human subjects repeatedly investigated their own hands, and this was often accompanied by overt sniffing (see online Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the video data.

claim: Sniffing of the right shaking hand significantly increased selectively following handshakes with same gender individuals.
source: Our analyses reveal that such sniffing of the right shaking hand significantly increased selectively following handshakes with same gender individuals, and we speculate that this reflects chemo-investigation of conspecifics.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The increased sniffing of the right shaking hand after same-gender handshakes reflects chemo-investigation of conspecifics.
source: Our analyses reveal that such sniffing of the right shaking hand significantly increased selectively following handshakes with same gender individuals, and we speculate that this reflects chemo-investigation of conspecifics.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Sniffing of the right shaking hand dropped to a level significantly below baseline following cross-gender handshakes.
source: Note that sniffing of the right shaking hand also persisted following cross-gender handshakes, yet here it dropped to a level significantly below baseline.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Humans are not only passively exposed to social chemosignals, but rather actively search for them.
source: Thus, this finding implies that humans are not only passively exposed to social chemosignals, but rather actively search for them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of hand-sniffing behavior observed.

claim: Putative chemosignals and an ordinary perfume drove opposite effects in the tainting experiment.
source: This was further evident in the tainting experiment where putative chemosignals and an ordinary perfume drove opposite effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: Previous studies found that AND and EST can bias perceptions in a gender-specific manner.
source: However, whereas previous studies found that AND and EST can bias perceptions in a gender-specific manner (Savic et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AND and EST drove similar effects within gender that were opposite to that of a standard perfume in the current study.
source: here AND and EST drove similar effects within gender that were opposite to that of a standard perfume.
evidence: This is a finding from the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: The behavior measured was influenced by unnoticed odor.
source: In other words, the behavior we measured was indeed influenced by unnoticed odor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the odor-tainting experiment combined with awareness data.

claim: The results were characterized by gender specificity that is common in social chemosignaling.
source: Our results were characterized by gender specificity that is common in social chemosignaling (Doty, 1986; Savic et al., 2001; Bensafi et al., 2003; Dulac and Torello, 2003; Brennan and Zufall, 2006; Bergan et al., 2014; Kaur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation about the results supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In rodents the chemosignal-mediated suppression of estrus is a within gender effect.
source: For example, in rodents the chemosignal-mediated suppression of estrus (Van Der Lee and Boot, 1955) is a within gender effect.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In humans, chemosignal-mediated menstrual synchrony is a within gender effect.
source: In humans, chemosignal-mediated menstrual synchrony (Stern and McClintock, 1998) is also a within gender effect.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The strong within gender effects observed in this study are not inconsistent with chemosignaling behavior.
source: Therefore, the strong within gender effects observed in this study are not inconsistent with chemosignaling behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison with prior research.

claim: The particular pattern of increased sampling within gender may be strongly modulated by context.
source: In turn, we speculate that the particular pattern we observed, namely increased sampling within gender, may be strongly modulated by context.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Human chemosignaling is not only gender-specific, but also sexual-orientation-specific.
source: Finally on this front, several studies imply that human chemosignaling is not only gender-specific, but also sexual-orientation-specific (Savic et al., 2005; Berglund et al., 2006; Lubke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sexual orientation data was not collected in this study.
source: We did not collect sexual orientation data, and therefore cannot say if the current within gender increase is strictly gender-specific, or perhaps also related to sexual orientation.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study design.

claim: The mechanism proposed serves to bridge the apparent gap between a role for social chemosignaling in ongoing human behavior and the lack of overt conspecific chemo-investigation.
source: The mechanism we propose serves to bridge the apparent gap between a role for social chemosignaling in ongoing human behavior and the lack of overt conspecific chemo-investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical contribution of the study.

claim: Humans likely evolved social chemosignal-sampling strategies.
source: Given these effects, which we speculate are only the tip of the iceberg, humans likely evolved social chemosignal-sampling strategies (Arzi et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Handshaking is one of the social chemosignal-sampling strategies humans evolved.
source: and we propose that handshaking is one of them.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the study.

claim: Social chemosignaling is not the sole functional aspect of handshaking.
source: That said, we are not suggesting that social chemosignaling is the sole functional aspect of handshaking.
evidence: This is a clarification of the scope of the claim.

claim: Handshake orchestration conveys assorted social information.
source: Handshake orchestration conveys assorted social information (Firth, 1972; Schiffrin, 1974), contained within shake duration, posture, and strength (Chaplin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Social chemosignaling may be a functional antecedent of handshaking.
source: We do argue, however, that social chemosignaling may be a functional antecedent of handshaking and that it remains a meaningful albeit subliminal component of handshaking behavior.
evidence: This is the main argument of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Social chemosignaling remains a meaningful albeit subliminal component of handshaking behavior.
source: We do argue, however, that social chemosignaling may be a functional antecedent of handshaking and that it remains a meaningful albeit subliminal component of handshaking behavior.
evidence: This is the main argument of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Sniffing of the left hand subserves self-recognition.
source: We speculate that this reflects an ongoing comparative process whereby sniffing of the left hand subserves self-recognition and sniffing of the right hand subserves the investigation of others.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential hand-sniffing patterns.

claim: Sniffing of the right hand subserves the investigation of others.
source: We speculate that this reflects an ongoing comparative process whereby sniffing of the left hand subserves self-recognition and sniffing of the right hand subserves the investigation of others.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential hand-sniffing patterns.

claim: After within gender handshakes humans significantly increase investigation of the hand that shook.
source: Moreover, in the current context, after within gender handshakes humans significantly increase investigation of the hand that shook.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Hand investigation is concurrent with pronounced sniffing.
source: This investigation is concurrent with pronounced sniffing
evidence: This is a finding from the nasal airflow measurement experiment.

claim: Hand investigation is slightly increased after tainting the greeting experimenter with a perfume.
source: slightly increased after tainting the greeting experimenter with a perfume
evidence: This is a finding from the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: Hand investigation is negated after tainting the greeting experimenter with putative social chemosignals.
source: yet is negated after tainting the greeting experimenter with putative social chemosignals.
evidence: This is a finding from the odor-tainting experiment.

claim: Handshaking may subserve sampling of social chemosignals.
source: This combination leads us to conclude that handshaking may subserve sampling of social chemosignals.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings.

claim: These results imply an extensive role for social chemosignaling, which persists mostly without awareness for the signaling process.
source: In addition to providing a functional framework for a common human behavior, these results imply an extensive role for social chemosignaling, which persists mostly without awareness for the signaling process.
evidence: This is a broader implication drawn from the study findings.

claim: All 281 subjects signed informed consent to procedures approved by the Wolfson Hospital Helsinki Committee.
source: All 281 subjects signed informed consent to procedures approved by the Wolfson Hospital Helsinki Committee.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval and consent procedures.

claim: All experiments were conducted in stainless-steel coated odorant non-adherent rooms subserved by high throughput HEPA and carbon filtration.
source: All experiments were conducted in stainless-steel coated odorant non-adherent rooms subserved by high throughput HEPA and carbon filtration that were specially designed for human olfaction experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental environment and controls.

claim: Three handshakes were measured on each of three consecutive days by each of the 10 participants for the GCMS analysis.
source: For the initial measurement of possible chemosignal transfer by handshake (Figure 1) we measured three handshakes, one on each of three consecutive days, by each of the 10 participants (i.e., total 30 handshakes).
evidence: This describes the methodology for the GCMS experiment.

claim: One subject used hand cream and one subject used facial cream in the GCMS study.
source: One subject (F) used hand cream and one subject (M) used facial cream.
evidence: This describes the cosmetic use in the GCMS study sample.

claim: GCMS analysis of the hand-soap did not find traces of any of the three components that occurred consistently across subjects.
source: We therefore conducted GCMS analysis of this soap, and did not find traces of any of the three components that occurred consistently across subjects.
evidence: This is a finding from the control GCMS analysis.

claim: The decision to score 1 min before and 1 min after the greeting event was an a priori decision and not the result of a fishing expedition for time windows.
source: We clearly state here that the decision to score 1 min before and 1 min after the greeting event (which culminated at ∼80 s given the added time of the greet event itself, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), rather than some other time window, was an a priori decision and not the result of a fishing expedition for time windows.
evidence: This is a methodological clarification about the analysis approach.

claim: The data were abnormally distributed (Skew = −2.46, Kurtosis = 11).
source: Because subjects who did not sample their hand both before and after the greet during this 1 min were scored at zero (0) change in duration, this rendered the data abnormally distributed (Skew = −2.46, Kurtosis = 11).
evidence: This describes a statistical property of the data.

claim: An ANOVA is relatively insensitive to abnormal distribution at sample sizes such as these.
source: Although an ANOVA is relatively insensitive to this at sample sizes such as these (Lix et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on statistical methods.
